name: TierHive
oneLiner: Build-your-own NAT KVM servers from $0.000135 an hour, with a private /24, two forwarded TCP ports and a shared HAProxy — cheap, hourly, and explicitly still in Alpha.
whatItIs: TierHive rents KVM virtual machines by the hour at the lowest end of the market. You do not pick from a plan list: you move sliders for RAM (128 MB to 8 GB in 128 MB steps), NVMe (1 to 50 GB) and, in four locations, HDD up to 4 TB, then choose a CPU-priority, IOPS and network tier. The smallest configuration, 128 MB of RAM with 1 GB of disk, is $0.000135 an hour — about ten cents for a 720-hour month.

The unusual part is the network. A server does not get its own public IPv4. Each account gets a private /24 that is meshed across locations, and each server gets two forwarded TCP ports and two UDP ports on the public address of the machine it runs on. The first TCP port is always mapped to the server's port 22, so SSH arrives on a random high port of a shared IP. Web traffic normally goes through the free shared HAProxy instead: you add a domain in the panel, point DNS at TierHive, and it terminates TLS with a Let's Encrypt certificate. An IPv6 /64 per location is also available, up to ten addresses per server, which opens nearly all ports and removes the NAT limit.

vCPU is not something you buy. A server with 2 GB of RAM or less gets one vCPU and anything larger gets two, so two is the ceiling. The CPU is shared and weighted by the priority tier you pay for, and a server that averages a full core for two hours is cut to half a core until it reboots.

Billing is prepaid: one token is one US dollar, the first top-up is $3, and each server bills its hourly rate with a one-hour minimum. The operator says a server that is powered off bills only its storage, and that deleting it ends the bill immediately. There is no monthly price and no monthly cap.

TierHive is candid about what it is not. Its acceptable-use policy says the service is in Alpha, that data loss can occur at any time without warning, that backups are the customer's responsibility, and that there is no SLA. The About page says it is a budget service on older hardware, that it is not the place to host anything you need uptime for, and that if data is lost you get a fresh, blank server rather than a recovery.
whoFor: Readers who want the cheapest possible Linux box for a hobby agent, a bot, a test box or a throwaway node, who can work a console, and who keep their own backups. Not for production, not for anything that needs a public IPv4 of its own, more than two vCPUs, or a promise about uptime.
isolation: A KVM virtual machine with its own kernel and root, on the operator's own QEMU/KVM/libvirt stack. CPU and disk I/O are shared and weighted, not dedicated; a server that averages a full core for two hours is throttled to half a core until it is rebooted.
sizes: Build your own: RAM 128 MB to 8 GB in 128 MB steps, NVMe 1 to 50 GB, HDD up to 4,000 GB in London, Singapore, Sydney and Vint Hill, plus backup and snapshot storage. vCPU is not a choice — one core up to 2 GB of RAM, two cores above it, never more. 8 GB is not available in every location (Tokyo tops out at 1 GB). 19 locations across Europe, North America, South America, Asia-Pacific and Africa.

billing.model: Prepaid hourly tokens at $1 each. No subscription and no monthly plan: you add credit and each server draws its hourly rate until you delete it. The first top-up is $3.
billing.meter: A per-hour price built from published resource rates — RAM $0.0009216 per GiB-hour, NVMe $0.00002 per GB-hour, HDD $0.000007, backup storage $0.000005, snapshots $0.00002 — plus optional priority tiers at $0.00002 (Medium) or $0.00003 (High) an hour each. The panel's own estimate uses 720 hours for a month.
billing.stopped: The operator says a powered-off server bills only its storage, and that deleting it stops the charge. A stop is a power-off, so memory and running processes are lost; nothing resumes where it left off. The stopped-state details are only in the operator's forum offers, not on tierhive.com.
billing.planFee: There is no platform fee and no plan. The only extra charges in the price feed are the DHCP fee (about $0.0007 a month), backup creation and restore fees, and backup or snapshot storage.
billing.minimum: One hour per server, and a $3 first top-up. A ten-minute server costs an hour; 1,000 ten-minute servers cost 1,000 hours.

A.headline: $3.89 a month, because every ten-minute server pays for an hour
A.shape: 4 GiB / 10 GB (2 vCPU), one server per task, each billed its one-hour minimum

lines.label: The work itself
lines.arithmetic: 1,000 × 10 min = 166.67 h, billed as 1,000 h at the one-hour minimum

notes: 4 GiB is the smallest size that gives 2 vCPU, so the shape matches the ask exactly; there is no CPU charge on top of RAM.

Each task is a separate server, created and deleted, so each one pays the one-hour minimum. Running them back to back on a single server would cost 166.67 hours ($0.65) instead — but that is one long-lived server, not 1,000 throwaway tasks.
Low-priority CPU, IOPS and network are free and are what the card prices. Adding Medium priority on all three would add $0.06 an hour.
The $3 first top-up covers most of this; a $4 balance covers it.
A.flag: The one-hour minimum is what makes A expensive here. If the provider ever meters the first hour by the minute, A falls to about 65 cents.

B.headline: $6.11 a month on 2 vCPU — the 4 vCPU asked for cannot be bought
notes: 8 GiB is the largest size sold, and it comes with two vCPU, not four.
8 GB is not offered in every location: Amsterdam, Beauharnois, Frankfurt, Gravelines, London, New York, Sydney and Vancouver list an 8,192 MB ceiling, while Tokyo tops out at 1,024 MB.
The CPU watchdog is irrelevant at 10% average load, but the CPU is shared and the provider warns of high steal.
The provider's own 720-hour month would be $6.03.
B.flag: Workload B asks for 4 vCPU. TierHive never gives more than 2, so this price is for the largest machine it sells, not the one the workload describes.

C.headline: $0.62 a month, and 41% of it is billed while the server is off
C.shape: 4 GiB / 20 GB (2 vCPU), 90 running + 640 stopped hours
notes: This is the shape TierHive is built for: three hours a day on a machine that keeps its files and costs a few cents a month.

The stopped line assumes the operator's forum statement that only storage bills while powered off. It is not on tierhive.com, and the exact stopped charges are unpublished. If stopped hours billed at the running rate, C would be $2.98.
A stop is a power-off: nothing keeps running and nothing resumes, so a process that has to be alive for three hours a day needs a start and a stop from outside.
The provider's own 720-hour month would be $0.62 too (630 stopped hours instead of 640).

well: A throwaway box for an experiment, a test deploy or a CI job: $0.003886 an hour for 4 GiB and 10 GB, deleted when the job ends.
A hobby agent, Discord or Slack bot, or small MCP server that needs a cheap always-on Linux box and can live behind a forwarded port or the shared HAProxy.
Three hours a day of work on a machine that keeps its files: about $0.62 a month at 4 GiB and 20 GB, most of it storage while stopped.
A homelab spread across 19 locations with a private /24 meshed between them, for WireGuard relays, monitoring probes or redundant small services.
badly: Anything that needs its own public IPv4, more than two forwarded TCP ports, or a fixed address other services can allowlist.
Anything with four or more vCPUs, more than 8 GB of RAM, a GPU or a dedicated core.
Production, or data you cannot lose: the operator's own policy says data loss can occur at any time and that there is no SLA.
A team that needs sub-users, SSO or an audit trail, or a buyer who needs a SOC 2 report or a data processing agreement.
Scraping at scale: the acceptable-use policy forbids automated scraping of external sites without prior written approval.

usability.dashboard: A custom control panel behind a login: create and rebuild servers, change RAM and disk, start and stop, map ports on the Subnet Config page, allocate IPv6, schedule backups and snapshots, add domains to HAProxy, and open a noVNC console.
usability.withoutCode: No. Creating a server is click-through and there are one-click recipes for Docker, WordPress, WireGuard and similar, but the recipes end at a console, ports are mapped by hand, and the HAProxy backend is your own private IP. Nothing here sets up an AI agent for you.
usability.signup: A username, email and password, then a six-digit code at every sign-in. No card is needed to register; the first tokens are bought through FastSpring with a $3 minimum. The terms forbid disposable email addresses and VPN sign-up, although the About page says the opposite.
usability.docs: Thin and blog-shaped: an About page, the acceptable-use policy, and 18 blog posts of which about a dozen are how-tos (finding your ports, HAProxy, IPv6, growing a disk, chrooting a backup). There is no knowledge base, no FAQ and no API reference.
tripsUp: There is no public IPv4 of your own: SSH arrives on a random high port of a shared address, and you get two forwarded TCP ports in total, one of which SSH already uses.
vCPU is not selectable. A 2 GB server has one core and anything larger has two, so a four-core machine cannot be bought at any price.
The one-hour minimum is charged per server, so a fleet of short-lived servers costs far more than the same work on one long-lived box.
The blog's hourly prices are stale: it quotes a Popular tier at $0.004061/h, which matches no current size.
Scraping needs written permission before you start, and bulk or transactional email is banned outright.
A stopped server is a power-off: nothing keeps running, and whether the stopped hours really bill storage only is stated in forum offers rather than on the site.
The service is in Alpha, with data loss and no SLA written into its own policy.

caveats.issue: Alpha, with data loss written into the policy
caveats.detail: The acceptable-use policy states that TierHive is in Alpha, that data loss can occur at any time without warning, that backups are the customer's sole responsibility and that those backups may also be lost. It tells customers not to use the service for production or critical data. The About page adds that if data is lost you get a fresh, blank server, not a recovery.

evidence.quote: Data loss can occur at any time without warning
in the event it happens, we will not recover it for you, you get a fresh, blank VPS

caveats.issue: Storage-only billing while stopped is not on the provider's website
caveats.detail: The operator's forum offers say a powered-off server bills only storage, and the pricing feed has no separate stopped rate. Nothing on tierhive.com describes the stopped state, so the card bills the NVMe rate for stopped hours and treats the rest as zero. If stopped hours billed at the running rate, C would rise from $0.62 to $2.98 (730 h × $0.0040864).

evidence.quote: You only pay for storage when the VPS is powered off.

caveats.issue: MB and GB look binary, not decimal
caveats.detail: The site calls the largest machine 8 GB while the price feed calls the same ceiling 8,192 MB, so its MB and GB are binary and its per-GB-hour disk rate maps 1:1 to this site's GiB. For RAM that is direct; for disk it is an inference, because no page defines the unit in bytes. If the disk GB is decimal, every disk charge is 7.37% higher — A $3.90, B $6.17, C $0.65 — and a 50 GiB disk would sit above the 50 GB ceiling.

evidence.quote: Up to 8GB RAM per VPS (not all locations support 8GB)

caveats.issue: Two forwarded TCP ports, and SSH takes one of them
caveats.detail: Every server gets two TCP and two UDP ports on the public address of its host, and the first TCP port is always mapped to port 22. That leaves one spare TCP port for anything else, which is why the provider's own HAProxy how-to uses a second VPS as a bastion. An IPv6 /64 per location, up to ten addresses per server, is the way around it — but the shared HAProxy does not serve IPv6.

evidence.quote: Your nat VPS is provided with 2 open TCP ports and 2 UDP port. By design the 1st TCP port is mapped to your VPS port 22/TCP.

caveats.issue: Free trial and a $3 minimum top-up are both advertised
caveats.detail: The homepage says a $3 minimum top-up is required after registration to use the service; the blog says to start with the free trial and no credit card; the price feed grants $0.01 of sign-up credit; the forum offers promise free tokens to try before buying. The honest reading is a free account with one cent of credit that may not be usable until $3 is added.

evidence.quote: A $3 minimum top up is required after registration to use this service.
Start with the free trial, no credit card required.

caveats.issue: The terms ban what the About page invites
caveats.detail: The terms forbid disposable email addresses and signing up over a VPN or proxy; the About page says the operator has no objection to a free or disposable email or a VPN. The terms also describe monthly or annual subscriptions, which is boilerplate from the company's other products — the actual product is prepaid hourly tokens.

evidence.quote: You may not use free or disposable email addresses to create or maintain an Account.
We have no objection to you using a free or disposable email, or a VPN

caveats.issue: A Sao Paulo location sits next to a ban on Brazilian customers
caveats.detail: The price feed lists Sao Paulo with a 4,096 MB ceiling, while the terms say the service cannot be provided to customers in Brazil (along with China, Russia, Vietnam and Iran). The node is real; customers located in Brazil are refused.

evidence.quote: We are unable to provide our Services to customers in the following countries: China, Russia, Brazil, Vietnam, and Iran.

caveats.issue: The marketing blog quotes prices that no longer exist
caveats.detail: The hourly-VPS explainer quotes a Popular tier at $0.004061/h, which reproduces from no current size, while the homepage's Popular card is $0.007561/h. Its Standard figure, $0.002343/h, still matches. No rate in this package comes from the blog.

evidence.quote: The Popular tier is $0.004061/hour. The Standard is $0.002343/hour.

caveats.issue: No documented API, CLI or SDK
caveats.detail: The site's sitemap lists every public page and there is no developer, API or CLI page; every guessed panel path returns 401 behind the login. The only public JSON endpoints are the marketing calculator's rate feed and the recipe ticker. A third-party dossier reaches the same conclusion. Nothing here says an API will never exist — only that none is documented today.

caveats.issue: Shared CPU with a watchdog and a fair-use network throttle
caveats.detail: The provider warns that CPU is the most contended resource, that steal will be higher than on an enterprise host, and that a server averaging a full core for two hours is limited to half a core until it reboots. Network speed is a tier (50 to 300 Mbit/s by location) that steps down by 10 Mbit/s an hour under sustained use, to a floor of 10 Mbit/s. Neither binds at the loads in A, B and C.

evidence.quote: We have a CPU watchdog: if you average 100% of a CPU core for more than 2 hours solid, you will be limited to 50% of a core on the backend.

caveats.issue: No SOC 2 report or data processing agreement is published
caveats.detail: The legal pages are terms, privacy, refunds and acceptable use. There is no DPA, no sub-processor list and no audit report. The company is UK-based; its EU locations are in Germany, France, the Netherlands and Poland. A buyer who needs GDPR paperwork should ask before buying.

strengths: The cheapest hourly Linux box in this guide: $0.000135 an hour for 128 MB and 1 GB, $0.003886 for 4 GiB and 10 GB.
Genuine per-resource pricing — RAM and disk are sliders, not plan steps — so a small machine is not forced to buy a large disk.
Storage-only billing while a server is powered off, which makes a three-hours-a-day machine cost cents rather than dollars.
A private /24 meshed across 19 locations, free shared HAProxy with Let's Encrypt, IPv6 /64s, and one-click recipes including Docker, WireGuard and WordPress.
An unusually candid operator: the limits, the lack of an SLA and the risk of data loss are all written down in public.
